tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. Exit code 1
Pipes on TinyGL: too slow as written, and what would change that
Pipes was the first GL hack tried and it is not viable on TinyGL as written.
Record what was learned and what would change that. Depends on #42; see also
#43. Data is in `docs/tinygl-spike.md` on branch `worktree-spike-tinygl`.

## Why it is slow

Pipes does not accumulate. Every frame it clears and redraws every piece so
far from display lists (`draw_pipes` loops over `system_index`), up to about
500 pieces per system with the defaults, under a slowly rotating camera. Cost
grows with the pipe, and every frame changes completely, so pushing only the
changed rows saves nothing.

With Pipes' real primitives (triangle-strip spheres of 16 by 16, 24-facet
quad-strip tubes), measured on the S3 at 464 by 464:

- 3.7 ms per piece, plus about 80 ms fixed per frame.
- 2.8 fps at 80 pieces, 1.2 fps at 210, under 1 fps by 250.
- Wireframe (`*wireframe: True`) is no faster: the same frame times, because
  the cost is per vertex and the wire sphere sends twice the vertices.
- 8 by 8 spheres (about 3.7 times fewer triangles) gave 5.2 fps at 50 pieces,
  3.4 at 100. Not enough on its own.

## What would change that

- Stop redrawing the settled scene. The camera turns only 0.02 degrees per
  frame, so drawing just the newest piece onto the existing frame, and
  redrawing everything only now and then, would make the cost per frame
  constant. Needs interception at the GL layer and slightly changes the look
  (the older pieces lag the camera).
- Faster vertex setup in TinyGL (#43).

## Port notes

- The real spheres come from `unit_sphere` in `sphere.c`, which builds
  `glVertexPointer` arrays and calls `glDrawArrays` inside a display list.
  TinyGL gets that wrong; the array shim from #42 fixes it.
- Pipes also needs `buildlwo.c`, `teapot.c` (built unconditionally),
  `sphere.c`, `gltrackball.c` and `rotator.c`. All are in `hacks/glx/`, so
  they can be copied byte-identical.
- Pipes uses two lights' state and a specular material.

### rodbegbie 2026-10-11T08:48:52Z
Overnight update from Claude, an agent working under Rod's direction (the
night of 2026-10-10 to 11). Host only: nothing has been flashed. The lab is
on branch `feature/44-pipes` in `docs/pipes-lab/` (its README has the
commands and the full table). It builds Pipes and its helpers straight from
`vendor/`, so nothing from Pipes is copied into the repo.

## The incremental redraw works, and is exact

`docs/pipes-lab/pipes_incremental.h` wraps Pipes' `glClear`, `glCallList`,
`glNewList`, `glEndList` and `glXSwapBuffers` (macros before the include; the
hack stays byte-identical). When the clear, the modelview and projection
matrices and the lists so far all match last frame, it skips the clear and
those lists and replays only the new ones. Anything else falls back to a real
clear and a full replay. Over 600 frames, every frame hash matched a full
redraw, both with the camera turning and with it fixed.

With `*rotatepipes: False` (fixed camera), steady frames set up about 300 to
380 vertices instead of up to 977,000, and the swap marks about 11 rows
instead of about 365. With the default turning camera every frame is a full
redraw, so the wrapper never skips.

## New blockers the lab found

- **Memory.** Pipes builds every display list of a screen when the screen
  starts. As written (`*cycles: 5`, `*size: 500`, about 2,500 pieces) that is
  about 44 MB of host heap, roughly 22 MB on the board (a list word is 8 bytes
  on the host and 4 on the board), against about 7 MB of free PSRAM.
  `*cycles: 1` with `*size: 100` is about 0.7 MB on the board; `*cycles: 2`
  with `*size: 150` about 2.3 MB.
- **The fade.** A screen ends with 25 frames that shrink the whole picture,
  so each is a full redraw: about 32,000 vertices at `size` 100 (roughly
  0.2 s a frame at #43's costs) and 977,000 as written.
- **Helpers TinyGL cannot run as copied.** `teapot.c` uses GL evaluators
  (`glMap2f`, `glEvalMesh2`); built with `HAVE_JWZGLES` it uses its triangle
  table (`teapot2.h`) instead. `buildlwo.c` draws `GL_POLYGON`, which this
  TinyGL drops, and the extra vertices overwrote the GL context (a crash on
  frame 16). The lab maps `GL_POLYGON` to `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN` for that file only.
  A general guard against the overwrite is on
  `fix/tinygl-unhandled-primitive`.
- **Licences.** `buildlwo.c`, `buildlwo.h`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` carry
  no licence text. The repo's precedent (Pacman's sprites, XMatrix's glyphs)
  is to read such files from `vendor/` at build time and never commit them.

## Decisions for Rod before a real port

1. A fixed camera (`*rotatepipes: False`): that is what makes the
   incremental redraw work.
1. Smaller screens (`*cycles: 1`, `*size: 100` to `200`), to fit PSRAM.
1. The fade: keep it (about 5 s of slow frames per screen at `size` 100), or
   end each screen without it, which the wrapper could do.
1. Build `buildlwo.c`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` from `vendor/` at build
   time, as the sprites are.

With those, steady frames would be a few milliseconds of GL work plus an
11-row push, so Pipes should run at the speed its own 10 ms pause allows.
That is an estimate; nothing has been measured on the board.

### rodbegbie 2026-10-11T19:18:05Z
Rod’s decisions:

1. Fixed camera is all good.
2. Let’s try this and see how it looks
3. End without the fade.  (We’ll come back to fades at a later date)
4. That’s the safest approach, but the `xscreensaver.spec` file says that the package is `License: BSD` so I’m not too worried about copying the files over.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/build/stopwatch-screensaver/.claude/skills/port-hack

# Porting an xscreensaver hack

The rules live in `AGENTS.md` ("Rules", "Gotchas") and the path-scoped notes in
`.claude/rules/`. This skill sets the order of work and the points to stop. The
numbered steps are in `adding-a-hack.md` and the recipes it names are in
`techniques.md`, both next to this file. For several hacks in one go, read
`batches.md` too.

## 1. Pick, then read the source

Take S-rated rows from `docs/porting-assessment.md` first, and prefer a low
**Speed** band: the table runs each unported S hack on the host. The effort
rating counts missing shim calls, not memory, speed or stack (Braid was S, and
would have shown as high). A high band is a hack that will probably run slowly
on the board; a low band is not a guarantee, because a hack still doing
software `double` maths runs far slower on the device than on the host. Read
the hack's source before copying it, and look for:

| The source has | Technique (seen in) |
| --- | --- |
| Arrays or a state over a few MB | Build-time patch (Maze) |
| `sin`, `cos`, `sqrt`, `pow`, `double` in a hot loop | Single precision (Galaxy, Substrate) |
| Locals over a few KB | Stack check (Rorschach) |
| An allocation of 100 KB or more, or `exit()` on failure | Large allocations (Substrate) |
| Pixmaps, clip masks, a logo image | Images (Maze) |
| A hack that restarts itself | Restart leak test (Maze, Substrate) |
| A `free` that relies on state `draw` sets up (a lazy `initted`) | Stopping before the first draw (Blaster) |
| Hairlines, fades or `glPolygonOffset` in a GL hack | Thin lines in a GL hack |
| Threads, GL, Xft, shared memory | Skipping a hack |
| A licence header | Read it; add a notices section only if it differs from jwz's |

## 2. Set up

Work in a worktree off `origin/main`. Its setup and the commands it refuses are
in "Worktree setup".

## 3. Red, copy, green

Follow `adding-a-hack.md`. Show the registry test failing before
copying. Fill each shim gap test-first, then break the code on purpose and
watch the test fail ("Tests that cannot be fooled"). Filling a missing
function is a shim gap. Changing what every hack sees (the runner, a default, a
shared helper) is not: stop and ask Rod first. A speed-up in the shared GL
layer counts too, even when every pinned frame hash still matches (HexTrail's
deferred depth clear): ask before writing it, and name it in the PR body.

Run `pio test -e native`, `uv run --with pytest --with pillow pytest tools/tests`
and `uv run tools/check_notices.py`, and dump frames at several counts. Host
frames cannot show a byte swap, which happens in the push to the display: judge
colour on the device, on a colour you know the answer to.

## 5. Device

Flash only after Rod says so in this conversation; approval for one flash is
not approval for the next. See "Device capture". Report "compiles", "host tests
pass" and "runs on the device" separately; only Rod can say what the screen
shows. If it is slow, measure, change one thing, flash again and compare; if it
is still slow, say so and suggest dropping it. A hack that runs at a good rate
can still go: Rod dropped Boing (8.3 fps, "pretty boring on a small screen")
and asked for HexTrail to be tuned because it fell under 10 fps before the
rotation moved on. Judge a hack on a 466 px round screen, and by its worst
window as well as its mean. Record the numbers in
`tools/assessment_measured.md.in`, marking anything unmeasured as such.

Commit named paths. Open the draft PR with `entire trail create` and put what
is unverified in its body. After a rebase, a push needs `--force-with-lease`:
ask Rod each time. Rod approves and merges; then delete the branch and
fast-forward `main`. New gotchas go in the matching `.claude/rules/` file (or
`AGENTS.md` if they apply everywhere) in the same PR, and deferred
ideas become issues.

## Red flags

| Thought | Reality |
| --- | --- |

| "AGENTS.md says to fix shim gaps, so I can change the runner" | A new function is a gap. A change every hack sees needs Rod. |
| "Rod approved flashing earlier" | Ask again for each flash. |
| "Single precision is done, so the hack is as fast as it gets" | HexTrail gained 0.3 fps from it and 2.3 from a depth clear in the GL layer. Read what the shared code does each frame. |
| "The mean is above 10 fps" | HexTrail's mean was 15.3 and its worst window 10.8; its step grew all cycle. Read the lowest window. |

# Pipes lab (issue #44)

A host-only experiment, not a port. It builds Pipes and its helpers straight
from `vendor/` against the shim and `tools/gl_budget.py`'s instrumented
TinyGL, and prints one line per frame: vertices, lit vertices, filled pixels,
the rows the swap marked, and a hash of the canvas.

```bash
python3 -I docs/pipes-lab/build.py /tmp/pipes --incremental \
    '*delay: 10000' '*ncolors: 64' '*cycles: 1' '*size: 100' \
    '*rotatepipes: False'
/tmp/pipes/prog 3000 1
```

Without `--incremental` it is Pipes as written. `HEAP=1` adds the host heap in
use after each frame; `ASAN=1` keeps AddressSanitizer on.

## What it changes, and why

- `pipes_incremental.h` is the experiment: an exact incremental redraw. Pipes
  clears and replays every piece's display list each frame, in order, under
  one camera, and adds one piece a frame. When the clear, both matrices and
  the lists so far match last frame, the canvas and z-buffer already hold
  them, so the wrapper skips the clear and those lists and replays only the
  new one. Anything else falls back to a real clear and a full replay.
- `teapot.c` is built with `HAVE_JWZGLES`, which picks its triangle table
  (`teapot2.h`) over GL evaluators (`glMap2f`, `glEvalMesh2`), which TinyGL
  lacks.
- `buildlwo.c` is built with `GL_POLYGON` mapped to `GL_TRIANGLE_FAN`. TinyGL
  is built without `GL_POLYGON`, and an unhandled primitive keeps counting
  vertices past `c->vertex[3]` and overwrites the context: the lab crashed on
  frame 16 in `first_light`.

## Results (host, seed 1)

Frames are identical with and without the wrapper: every frame hash matched
over 600 frames, with the camera turning (the default, where the wrapper never
skips) and with it fixed.

| Settings | Extra host heap | Steady vertices a frame | Fade vertices a frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| As written (`cycles` 5, `size` 500), full redraw | about 44 MB | up to 977,000 | 977,000 |
| As written, incremental, camera fixed | about 44 MB | 380 | 977,000 |
| `cycles` 1, `size` 100, incremental, fixed | 1.2 to 1.7 MB | 307 | 32,200 |
| `cycles` 1, `size` 200, incremental, fixed | 2.7 to 3.6 MB | 327 | 69,800 |
| `cycles` 2, `size` 150, incremental, fixed | 4.4 to 4.9 MB | 321 | 100,400 |

- Extra heap is over a `size` 10 run (3.2 MB), and is mostly display lists.
  A list word (`GLParam`) holds a pointer, so it is 8 bytes on the host and 4
  on the board: halve these for the board. Pipes as written needs about 22 MB
  there, and the board has about 7 MB of PSRAM free. Pipes builds every list
  of a screen when the screen starts.
- A screen ends with a 25-frame fade that scales the whole picture, so every
  fade frame is a full redraw. At the #43 costs (4 us a vertex, 2.8 us more
  for each light on each lit vertex) a 32,200-vertex fade frame is about
  0.2 s.
- With the default turning camera every frame is a full redraw, so the
  wrapper never helps.

None of this has run on the board.

## Open decisions

- `buildlwo.c`, `buildlwo.h`, `pipeobjs.c` and `teapot2.h` carry no licence
  text. The repo's precedent for such files (Pacman's sprites, XMatrix's
  glyphs) is to read them from `vendor/` at build time and never commit them.
- A fixed camera (`*rotatepipes: False`) changes the look.
- The fade: keep it (about 5 s per screen at `size` 100), or end a screen
  without it.
- `GL_POLYGON` and `GL_LINE_LOOP` in TinyGL generally (see the #44 comment).

      52 docs/pipes-lab/lab_main.c
     115 docs/pipes-lab/pipes_incremental.h
      70 docs/pipes-lab/README.md

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is

# GL layer and TinyGL gotchas

OpenGL hacks run on TinyGL, a software OpenGL (C-Chads fork, commit
`36a7987`, zlib-style licence). Issues #42 to #46 hold the numbers and ideas.

- `src/tinygl/` is byte-identical to upstream and excluded from every env.
  `firmware/patch_tinygl.py` runs `tools/tinygl_patch.py` and writes the
  patched tree, plus one unity file, into `.pio/build/<env>/generated/`;
  `glshim/tinygl_build.c` compiles it. Each patch checks its anchor and fails
  with "has upstream changed?". TinyGL's README allows building it as one
  unit, and it compiles cleanly that way.
- A GL hack gets `USE_GL` from a one-line wrapper: `hacks/<name>_gl.c` for
  the hack, `glshim/glx_<name>.c` for each helper copied to
  `xs_support/glx/`. Exclude the copies in all three envs' `build_src_filter`
  and keep `-Isrc/xs_support/glx` in `build_flags`. Never define `HAVE_GL`:
  it adds `glx_context` to `ModeInfo`, which `xlockmore.c` (built without
  it) allocates smaller. Build each helper as its own unit: `tube.h` and
  `normals.h` define clashing types.
- TinyGL draws straight into `canvas->px` at the canvas size, with its
  pixel packer patched to the canvas's byte-swapped RGB565. Test colours
  with exact `rgb565()` values: white looks the same either way round.
- Display list name 0 means "invalid" to hacks (`if (!glGenLists(1)) abort()`)
  and TinyGL handed it out first; the patch starts at 1. Its list buffers
  are 64 slots, not 4,096: each list took 16 KB and 500 lists overflowed
  PSRAM (boot loop, `StoreProhibited` at `0x4000` in `alloc_list`).
- TinyGL counts vertex-array stride in floats and reads the array when a
  display list is replayed; GL counts bytes and reads at the draw call, and
  hacks free the array straight after (`tube.c`, `sphere.c`). Hacks'
  `glVertexPointer` and friends are renamed to `glshim_*` by macros in
  `glshim.h`, and `glDrawArrays` expands at once. The symptom of the old
  behaviour was needles through the tubes.
- The context is freed by the shim: `glshim_open` registers
  `xshim_set_release_hook`, which `xshim_release_pixmaps` (the runner's
  `stop()`) runs. A second `init_GL` replaces the first, which hides a
  missing hook, so test `glshim_is_open()` right after the hack stops.
- `glshim_open` returns NULL for an empty canvas or a failed z-buffer
  allocation only. `glInit`'s own allocations (lists, matrix stacks) are
  unchecked upstream, so running out of PSRAM after the z-buffer crashes there.
- `glDrawArrays` reads every client array as `GL_FLOAT` and ignores the type
  argument: check a new hack's `glVertexPointer` calls before trusting it.
- TinyGL leaves specular lighting off (`zEnableSpecular = 0`) unless the
  application calls `glSetEnableSpecular(1)`, so Gears has no highlights
  and `glMateriali` is invisible without it. Enabling it costs speed (#43).
- TinyGL is built without `GL_POLYGON` (`TGL_FEATURE_GL_POLYGON 0`), which
  upstream also uses to compile out `GL_LINE_LOOP`. `tinygl_patch.py` puts the
  line loop back (issue #80): StonerView's squares now have their outlines.
  `GL_POLYGON` still draws nothing. Unknown Pleasures' rim loop is drawn too,
  but sits at depth -0.015 behind the slab's top face (-0.01), so no frame
  changed. An unhandled primitive used to keep counting vertices, and the fifth
  overwrote the matrices and colours after `c->vertex` (Pipes' `buildlwo.c`
  crashed the host); `tinygl_patch.py` now holds it at the first slot. Check a
  new hack for both.
- TinyGL lacks `glTexGeni`, `glFog*` and `glInterleavedArrays` (#46). The
  header declares `glFog*` and the `GL_SPHERE_MAP` enum; the library defines
  neither.
- TinyGL snaps every vertex to a whole pixel (`zp.x`, `zp.y`) before it draws,
  so a line that moves a little jumps a whole pixel somewhere along its length:
  Unknown Pleasures' flat stretches hopped, which read as flicker. The patch
  keeps the fractional position (`zp.fx`, `zp.fy`) and draws a line with Wu's
  algorithm when a hack enables `GL_LINE_SMOOTH`. Only lines get it; filled
  triangles are still snapped. A line whose two colours differ is drawn plain.
- Smooth lines ignore vertex alpha (`ZB_line_aa` reads only r, g, b), so
  Unknown Pleasures' per-row fade (`glColor4f` with an eased alpha) does not
  happen and every ridge draws at full intensity. Rod approved that look on the
  device and closed the review finding as wontfix.
- TinyGL has no alpha: the blend macro adds colours, ignores the blend
  function's alpha, and decodes pixels as if they were not byte-swapped, so
  it is only right for black and white. A white-on-black frame hides this, and
  smooth (grey) lines did not. The fill wrapper (`gl_draw_triangle_fill` in
  `tinygl_patch.py`) treats `SRC_ALPHA, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA`, which is alpha 1
  in real GL, as an opaque fill. A blend that only adds (each factor `GL_ONE`
  or one TinyGL treats as one, such as StonerView's `GL_SRC_ALPHA, GL_ONE`,
  with `GL_FUNC_ADD`) takes `glshim_add565`, a saturating add per channel on
  the swapped pixel (`TGL_BLEND_ADDS` in `tinygl_patch.py`); StonerView's
  colours went from scattered dark and rainbow squares to smooth runs of hue,
  and Rod preferred them. The other blend functions still use the macro and
  are wrong for any colour but black and white.
- Polygon offset was stored and never read. The fill wrapper applies it:
  `factor` times the polygon's steepest depth slope plus `units` times one
  depth step, pushed away from the viewer. Without it a line drawn on the edge
  of its own filled polygon is erased in dashes. Unknown Pleasures' own
  `glPolygonOffset (0.5, 0.5)` is not enough here: vertices are snapped to
  whole pixels, so a polygon's depth is wrong by up to a pixel's slope in each
  direction, and with only the hack's offset each quad still ate a few percent
  of its own line, a different few each frame. The wrapper adds
  `|dz/dx| + |dz/dy|` whenever an offset is asked for (not for an offset of 0, 0).
  Measured on the host by the second difference of a frame's total brightness
  while the picture drifts a fifth of a pixel a frame: 3,201 at the hack's own
  offset, about 500 (the floor) with the margin. An earlier depth-fighting
  experiment found no effect only because blending made every quad invisible:
  change one thing at a time, and check that the thing under test can act.
- The offset's snapping margin takes the sign of the offset (a negative offset
  pulls toward the viewer, so a positive margin would weaken it), the bias is
  clamped to about +/-2^29, and each shifted vertex depth is clamped to the
  16-bit range with the originals restored exactly: an offset that carried a
  fill past the far plane used to wrap round and beat a nearer fill. Tests use
  a second fill slightly behind the first, because a twin at equal depth wins
  a tie either way and cannot tell the signs apart.
- The clipper keeps lines inside the view volume, and the viewport maps NDC 1 to
  pixel `xsize - 0.5`, so only a viewport larger than the canvas can carry a
  line past its right or bottom edge. The smooth-line plot's guards are
  defensive otherwise; `test_glshim` uses `glViewport(0, 0, 2 * SIZE, 2 * SIZE)`
  to reach them.
- Speed is about 6 us per lit vertex plus about 80 ms a frame (clear 25 ms,
  push 32 ms): Gears runs at 4 to 5 fps for its heaviest layout and about 9
  for light ones. `-O2` for TinyGL and specular lookup tables changed
  nothing; whole-firmware `-O2` crashes the compiler in `braid_single.c`.
  `CLIP_EPSILON` was an exponent literal (`1E-5`), which `float_literals.py`
  leaves alone, so `gl_clipcode` ran a software `double` multiply on every
  vertex; `tinygl_patch.py` now makes it `1E-5f`, which took 5.6 ms off
  CubicGrid's 52 ms step (0.7 us a vertex) and about 3 ms off Morph3D's.
  `gl_shade_vertex` has not been checked for `double` the same way.
- Gears picks a random layout on each start, so a running Gears holds 0.9 to
  2.5 MB. Measure leaks while stopped, not by comparing two running moments.
  `free_gears` never frees `bp->gears`: 40 to 1,500 bytes a start, upstream.
- The host stack figure for Gears (21 KB, unoptimised and under
  AddressSanitizer) is not the board's (2.4 KB used in the spike); the host
  test is a tripwire and the board is the proof.
- `dump_main.c` raw frames are already un-swapped; `rgb565_to_png.py` reads
  them as plain RGB565. Swapping them again gives psychedelic stripes.
- `tools/gl_budget.py` counts vertices, triangles and fill in a private,
  instrumented copy of TinyGL (`instrument()` adds the counters after
  `tinygl_patch.patch_tree`, with the same checked anchors). The firmware's
  TinyGL never has them. Its fill cost is fitted to one Gears scene, so it
  over-predicts few-large-triangle scenes, and lines and points cost nothing
  beyond vertex setup. Add a second calibration point after each GL port.
- TinyGL's `glLightModelfv` copied four floats whatever the parameter, so
  `glLightModelfv(GL_LIGHT_MODEL_TWO_SIDE, one_float)` (Morph3D) read past the
  array: AddressSanitizer's global-buffer-overflow. `tinygl_patch.py` now copies
  four only for `GL_LIGHT_MODEL_AMBIENT`. `glopLightModel` still reads the
  value back as an int from a float slot, which only works because any
  non-zero float has non-zero bits; leave it unless a hack passes 0.
- Morph3D is small and wanders by design: a window (not iconic) build scales
  the object to 0.3 and moves it on a Lissajous path, so it is about 70 px
  across on the 466 px canvas and its position differs frame to frame. It
  cannot be enlarged without patching the hack. It enables two lights and
  two-sided lighting; `docs/gl-budget.md` predicts 6 to 11 fps.
- Dirty rectangle: TinyGL reports the box around everything it draws to
  `glshim_note_box` (hooks in `tinygl_patch.py`: triangles, points, lines,
  text pixels, and `glDrawPixels` as the whole canvas). `glClear` clears only the
  box drawn since the last clear and a swap marks only what was drawn and what
  the clear erased. A new context, and a new clear colour, are full clears. The
  contract: nothing else may draw on the canvas while a GL hack runs (the overlay
  restores what it stamps). A line's hook must order its endpoints before adding
  the margin: `p1.x - 1` to `p2.x + 1` shrinks a right-to-left line's box.
  `tools/gl_budget.py` gets its boxes from `glshim_box_observer` so it cannot
  drift from the firmware's rule.
- The round panel (issue #77): when the canvas has a disc, `glshim_open`
  exports its spans at TinyGL's size (`glshim_span_x0/x1`; at scale 2 a pixel
  counts if any of its 2 by 2 block does). `glClear` (colour and depth) and the
  scale-2 swap skip the corners, and `tinygl_patch.py` cuts each fill scanline
  to the span, advancing depth and colour to the new first pixel. The clip is
  decided once per triangle: the disc is convex, so a triangle with every vertex
  inside needs none. Checking every scanline cost Gears 3.2 ms a frame though it
  never reaches the corners; per triangle it costs 0.46 ms (58.27 to 58.73).
  HexTrail went from 48.62 to 45.32 ms, CubicGrid's clear from 12.3 to 10.0 ms.
  Textured fills (their own `DRAW_LINE`), lines and points are not clipped.
  Host test canvases have no disc, so pinned hashes are unchanged;
  `test_push_present` replays every hack on a disc canvas and compares only the
  disc. `gl_budget.py` counts fill without a disc, so it overstates corner fill.
- `glDrawPixels` keeps its data pointer in a 4-byte `GLParam`, so it cannot draw
  on a 64-bit host (fine on the 32-bit board); it has a patch-level test only.
- A hack's own `*delay` is a pause after each frame and the loop credits only the
  push against it, so it hides speed-ups: Morph3D (40 ms) and Gears (30 ms) were
  held to 10 and 11 to 13 fps until their registered override cut it to 10 ms.
  Check `wait=` in the log before judging a speed-up.
- Measuring on the board: a boot is deterministic (same hack, same layout, same
  windows), so alternate builds and compare window by window; one earlier
  outlier read 54.9 ms against 52.3 and was never explained. CubicGrid (fixed
  8,000 unlit points) and Gears' first layout after boot are the repeatable
  benchmarks; Morph3D's shape is random per boot. To split a frame, add a
  temporary `#if GL_PROFILE == n` early return to a TinyGL function through
  `tinygl_patch.py` and flash with `-DGL_PROFILE=n`; never commit it.
- A `glClear` of the depth buffer while the depth test is off does nothing
  until the test is enabled (`glshim_depth_test_changed`, patched into
  `misc.c`): nothing reads depth with the test off, and the clear is a second
  full-canvas fill of PSRAM. HexTrail clears it every frame and never enables
  the test; skipping it took 13.0 fps to 15.3. `glshim_depth_clears()` counts
  the clears that ran, for the tests.
- TinyGL has `glOrtho` commented out of its header (Boing needs it). `glshim.c`
  builds the usual matrix and calls `glMultMatrixf`; `test_glshim` checks it
  with an off-centre, non-square box and with the near and far planes, since
  ordering two triangles alone could not tell the depth term was wrong.
- Boing on TinyGL: its smooth, blended scanlines and shadow are the slow part

  and the board took 204 (171 step, 32 push): add that as a calibration point,
  since the model has no blend term. HexTrail was predicted at 15.7 fps for
  its early frames at count 20 and the first window on the board read 15.0,

  cycle (the step reached 293 ms).
- Overlapping the push with the next frame (core 0 pushing while core 1
  renders) is untried; it needs a second 434 KB buffer, a lock around M5GFX, and

  tabulates the windows. Each variant needs its own build directory:

  change. Gears' boot layout: fill 28 ms, vertex work outside lighting
  17 ms, clear 6 ms, lighting 3.7 ms of a 61 ms step.
- Lazy lighting is the default (`GL_LAZY_SHADE`; `-DGL_EAGER_SHADE` restores

- Every `Replace` anchor in `tinygl_patch.py` must be upstream text: the
  anchor tests delete it from the unpatched source. To add next to text an
  earlier patch inserted, extend that patch's replacement instead.

  can span the ends of `REPLACEMENTS`, `LATE_REPLACEMENTS` and `HOT_FUNCTIONS`,

  `GL_V3F`, `GL_C3F_V3F` and `GL_N3F_V3F` (what `gllist.c` uses);

/* Builds the unmodified blaster.c with a free that is safe before the first
 * draw. The hack sets NUM_ROBOTS in init but allocates `robots` on its first
 * draw, and its free loops NUM_ROBOTS times over `robots`, so freeing it first
 * dereferences NULL. Two quick button presses can do that. */
#include "screenhack.h"

/* blaster.c registers itself at its end; this file registers it instead. */
#undef XSCREENSAVER_MODULE
#define XSCREENSAVER_MODULE(CLASS, PREFIX)

#include "blaster/blaster.c"

static void blaster_free_safe(Display *dpy, Window window, void *closure) {
  struct state *st = (struct state *)closure;
  if (!st->robots) st->NUM_ROBOTS = 0;
  blaster_free(dpy, window, closure);
}

const HackEntry blaster_hack = {"Blaster", blaster_defaults, blaster_init,
                                blaster_draw, blaster_free_safe};

content.content:
# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).
- Braid runs at 3-9 fps (0.8-2 before four rounds of work): it redraws every
  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.
- A hack can be freed before its first draw: two quick presses, or a press
  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`
  runs every hack through it. Blaster's free dereferenced NULL (it sizes a loop
  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a
  free that zeroes `NUM_ROBOTS` when `robots` is NULL.
- Deluxe is built through `hacks/deluxe_opaque.c`, which includes the unmodified
  hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with overrides:
  `*transparent: False` (upstream's plane masks need colour planes, which
  `allocate_alpha_colors` reports none of) and `*doubleBuffer: False` (it was
  added when the shim drew only on the canvas, so the `XCopyArea` from its
  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).
  The wrapper then gives each throbber's GC an alpha of 26
  of 32 (upstream's translucent weight) and sends full wide circles to
  `stroke_circle`. A plain screenhack's `HackEntry` has no overrides unless a
  wrapper builds it. Its step is 45-63 ms on the device against a 32.5 ms push,
  so about 11-13 fps; ideas for more are in issue #54.
- Eight of the S-hack batch (Anemone, Anemotaxis, Compass, FuzzyFlakes,
  Halftone, Interaggregate, LMorph, Wormhole) are built through
  `hacks/<name>_direct.c` (pixmap double buffering, see `techniques.md`;
  LMorph's is `lmorph_single.c` because it needs no `HAVE_JWXYZ`). All but
  Anemotaxis and Wormhole, and Euler2D (`euler2d_single.c`), also use
  `single_precision.h` plus build-time float literals (`patch_float_literals.py`
  lists them). `single_precision.h` leaves `floor` and `ceil` on the double
  versions: Euler2D's wrapper maps them itself. After the literal pass, `nm`
  still shows soft-double helpers in Euler2D, Halftone, Interaggregate and
  Anemone; their source was not chased.
- `test_frames_of_every_hack_but_maze_match_main` stops at the first hash that
  differs, in registry order, so repinning several hacks takes one test run
  each (about 85 s), earliest first. A hack whose frames do not change under a
  wrapper (Compass and Halftone in single precision) keeps its hash.
- Anemone's step moves between 31 and 56 ms as its arms grow and shrink, so its
  fps is 11 to 15.5 whatever one 20 s window says. Forest waits 500 ms between
  trees by design (about 2 fps, and the push is 88 rows).
- A hack that unpacks pixel values itself (Substrate and Interaggregate, in
  their `point2rgb`) assumes ordinary RGB565, but the canvas holds the bytes
  swapped. Its wrapper swaps pixels where they cross `XAllocColor` and
  `XSetForeground`. Interaggregate shipped without this: its alpha blends
  mixed the wrong bit fields and drew rainbow noise instead of green and brown
  strokes. `test_interaggregate_blend` includes the wrapper to check one blend.
- `dump` never seeds `random()`, so a hack that picks a mode at start (Truchet,
  12 modes) shows the same one in every dump. To see others, build the hack
  alone (`probe_hacks.registry_source` and `shim_sources`) from a copy outside
  `vendor/`, with a `__attribute__((constructor))` that calls
  `srandom(atoi(getenv("SEED")))`. Cheaper: drop a temporary
  `src/hacks/zz_seed_tmp.c` with that constructor, guarded by `SEED` being set
  (`-e dump` builds every file under `src/`), run
  `SEED=n .pio/build/dump/program <index> <frames> out.raw`, and delete the
  file before running the tests. A device boot is deterministic too (Halo
  chose Ramp on five boots in a row), so a hack that picks a mode with
  `random()` always starts the same one: force another with a temporary
  `*mode:` override to measure it. Rotation reaches other modes because the
  random state differs by then.
- Hexadrop (`hexadrop_single.c`) runs at about 10 fps, under the 15 fps bar.
  Splitting its step on the device showed the maths and the edge walk cost
  0.1 ms and all the rest is canvas writes: about 860 KB of 16-bit stores
  into the PSRAM canvas a frame. Single precision, a float convex fill and
  two-pixel stores took it from 2.4 to 10.2 fps with pixel-identical frames.
  More needs a shared canvas change or rasterising in row bands.
- Halo (`halo_direct.c`, `halo_planes.h`, `halo_circles.h`) draws whole circles
  into 1-bit pixmaps and XORs two of them. Its pixmaps are packed bit planes
  (27 KB each), not colour pixmaps: 434 KB colour stand-ins made Seuss mode
  (three runs in four) 5-9 fps, because window-sized circles are millions of
  PSRAM writes, and a float circle fill alone changed nothing. A device boot
  is deterministic, so every boot picked Ramp mode and hid that: force
  `*colorMode: seuss` temporarily to measure the other mode. It overrides
  `*delay` to 10 ms (upstream asks for 100 ms), so the circles grow faster.
- StonerView's seven files are built as one unit by `stonerview_gl.c`.
  Upstream never frees its oscillator list ("how do we free this?"), so the
  wrapper frees it through the `next` links before upstream's release.
- XMatrix needs `matrix_glyphs.py` (a `pre:` script in every env), which
  converts four PNGs from `vendor/` into blobs in the build directory: they
  are never committed (1.5 MB of C text each for the large sheets). It
  registers through `xmatrix_direct.c` with `*trace: False`, which skips the
  typed "connecting" sequence it would open with (the rare "Knock, knock,
  Neo" event, `knockKnock`, is still on); `*matrixFont: small`
  gives 46 columns instead of 23. Its text modes read no text: the
  `textclient.h` stand-in never opens a source, and Xt timers never fire.
- Flurry is not ported. It draws 3,600 blended, textured quads a frame and
  needs `glAlphaFunc`, `glRectd`, `gluBuild2DMipmaps` and luminance-alpha
  textures, none in TinyGL here. With `gl_budget.py`'s per-vertex and
  per-pixel costs that is well under 1 fps (arithmetic, not a measurement:
  the tool cannot read a multi-file hack).
- Qix and Fireworkx both leaked on every stop, found by the restart leak test.
  Qix's `qix_free` skips each segment's `lines[i].p` array (about 48 KB per
  stop); Fireworkx below 24 bits never frees its own 565 image buffer (48 KB).
  Their wrappers (`qix_direct.c`, `fireworkx_single.c`) free the missing piece
  before calling upstream's free. LeakSanitizer does not run on macOS, but
  `MallocStackLogging=1 leaks --atExit -- .pio/build/dump/program <index> 0
  out.raw` names the allocating line in seconds (rebuild `-e dump` first: a
  `pio test` deletes the program).

  maths per edge per row). `hacks/float_polygon.h` fills any even-odd polygon

  channels with one multiply), and took Starfish from 8.5 to 19 fps. Goop draws
  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is still double
  (Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.

  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.

  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.

  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row

  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.

  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in

  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.

  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim

  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.

  30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s instead of 12.

  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).

  it back, add `pre:gl_textures.py` to the three `extra_scripts` and

  again. It drew 400 blocks

  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);
  fog is applied per block from the modelview's z when the hack
  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is
  no sphere map, so each face shows the whole texture. Its texture is
  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters

  frame.

  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:
  about 71,000 vertices a cube, three cubes by default. Floppy's model is
  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).

  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.
  Rocks stamps every rock bigger than 3 pixels with `XCopyPlane` from a
  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into
  a bitmap, so only the far dots showed (a 3,000-frame dump looked nearly
  black): `XFillRectangle` and `XFillPolygon` now fill bitmaps. On the board it

  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears
  the picture `load_image_async_simple` paints (see `x11shim.md`); without one
  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.

  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,
  all looked at).
- Abstractile holds about 6.1 MB of PSRAM while it runs (the free PSRAM read
  883 KB), so it leaves little for anything else: it stops and restarts clean
  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3
  fps) with frames that look the same but hash differently. Worm's worms are
  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.

# Per-hack gotchas

Moved verbatim from the Gotchas section of AGENTS.md.

- Maze keeps a 1000 by 1000 maze and three 1,000,000-entry move lists in one
  `calloc` (about 20 MB; the board has 8 MB of PSRAM). `hacks/maze/maze.c`
  stays byte-identical: `firmware/patch_maze.py` (a PlatformIO `pre:` script
  in every env) writes a copy with both limits at 80 into the build dir, using
  `tools/maze_patch.py`, which fails loudly if upstream's `#define`s change.
  `hacks/maze_small.c` includes that copy and the original is excluded from
  `build_src_filter`. A `gridSize` below 7 would overflow the 80 by 80 arrays.
- Pacman has two build-time patches (`tools/pacman_patch.py`, run by
  `firmware/patch_pacman.py`; wrappers `hacks/pacman_stdlevel.c` and
  `hacks/pacman_loop_ai.c`): the random level generator recursed to ~315 KB
  and boot-looped the board, so a generated level is a copy from
  `hacks/pacman_pool.h` (24 levels, made on the host by
  `tools/pacman_levels.py` with the cells outside the round display walled
  off; the fixed level is still half of them), and the ghosts' route search is
  a loop (it was 453 levels deep). Re-run the tool after changing its mask or
  the generator's tile data. Each patch checks what it replaces. The two host
  pins that follow the game (`kBaseline`'s Pacman and the ghost-route chain)
  depend on how many `random()` values the level pick takes: re-take the chain
  with `pacman_loop_ai.c` temporarily including `pacman/pacman_ai.c`, then
  restore it and check the loop gives the same value. Its sprite sheet is
  built from `vendor/` into the build dir by `firmware/pacman_sprites.py` and
  never committed (3 MB as C text).

  segment of the braid each frame to spin the colours. A host profile put its
  disc fill at 6% and the board spent most of its time there, because the Mac
  does `double` at full speed. Split a slow hack's step on the device with a
  temporary flag that returns early from the expensive call.
- Maze fills the whole 466 by 466 square, so its corners and the exit marker
  fall outside the round display's visible circle.
- `check_notices.py` reads 100 lines of header: Maze's licence follows a long
  modification history.

  with the 90 s rotation. `test_every_hack_can_be_stopped_before_its_first_frame`

  in init but allocates in draw), so `hacks/blaster_safe.c` includes the
  unmodified hack with `XSCREENSAVER_MODULE` emptied and registers it with a

  blank pixmap erased the picture; pixmaps work now, but two 434 KB back
  buffers and a full-frame copy each frame would cost more than they give).

  straight onto the window (its `XCreatePixmap` is the window and the
  `XCopyArea` is skipped) and blends each blob in at the alpha upstream's jwxyz
  path uses. Its full-frame clear cost 15 ms, so `hacks/span_erase.h` erases
  only the bounding boxes the blobs filled last frame (pixel-identical frames):
  14.6-15.2 fps translucent. The shared `canvas_fill_polygon` is still double
  (Hexadrop has its own convex float fill). Goop is built through
  `goop_direct.c` with `HAVE_JWXYZ`; the colour-plane path needs planes the
  canvas lacks.
- A wrapper that does `#define double float` must include any header with a
  `double` in a struct the shim's `.c` files also use BEFORE the define: the
  hack includes it again, the guard keeps the copy seen through the macro, and
  the two sides disagree on the layout. `spline.h` did this to Starfish and
  Goop: they drew garbage (flat colours) at 16-20 fps and their first pinned
  hashes were of it. Look at a frame after any change that is not
  pixel-identical by construction;
  `test_hacks_that_use_the_spline_draw_a_real_picture` now fails on a flat
  screen.
- Fireworkx renders at 1/`FIREWORKX_SCALE` of the width and height
  (`hacks/lowrez_put.h`: it is told the window is smaller and `XPutImage`
  draws each pixel as a square): 2.4 fps as copied, 11 at a scale of 3, 12.4 at
  4. Its glow, flash pass and 565 conversion are full-frame walks over PSRAM.
  Its header says "(GPL)" but the text is the standard permission notice.
  Everything it works in is in pixels, tuned for a window about 1024 wide: at
  152 pixels a burst filled the picture and the glow blur (energy kept, output
  doubled) saturated, so the screen was white. `tools/fireworkx_patch.py`
  (run before the float literal pass; the copy stays byte-identical) scales the
  spark speed, gravity, flash reach and velocity jitter by the render width
  over 1024, and the wrapper throws 120 sparks a shell instead of 500 and fires
  two of its four shells. 12.4-12.6 fps, with a dark background between
  bursts. The shell count cannot change (it is baked into the SSE layout), so
  the idle shells are given an endless life and no sparks.

  registry overrides it to 50 ms. It also took `malloc(0)` returning NULL, which
  the board does and the host does not, for out of memory: square mode asks
  for a rectangle list for each of eight colour states, most empty, and it
  freed its cells and drew nothing more (a black screen at 18 fps, half the
  starts, never seen on the host). `loop_direct.c` asks for one byte, and a test
  swaps in an allocator that returns NULL for zero. Hypnowheel was dropped from
  the rotation after Rod saw it, twice (issue #73; its source, notices row and a
  `failed_ports.txt` entry stay). `hypnowheel_single_gl.c` registers it only
  with `-DHYPNOWHEEL_PROBE`, as the last entry, for measuring. A board profile
  showed about 275 ms of its 706 ms step was `double` trig in every vertex, not
  fill as first thought; single precision gives 2.2 fps. The rest is fill
  (about 334 ms): `-DHYPNOWHEEL_HALF` renders at half resolution
  (`glshim_set_render_scale`) for 4.0 fps, still too slow for Rod.

  every store lands on a different cache line of the PSRAM canvas: after single
  precision took the step from 95 to 61 ms, 57 of those were the fills and 4
  the cosines. The picture depends on x alone, so the wrapper writes each
  full-height column into canvas row 0 and the draw wrapper copies that row
  down (frames identical to the unmodified hack): 16 ms, 20 fps. Any hack that
  paints thin full-height strips can do the same.

  one of its own `double` locals to a shim function (`rgb_to_hsv (..., &fgs,
  &fgv)` in Moire): the prototype still says `double *`, so the float local is
  written eight bytes and the frames come out as colour noise, with no
  compiler warning. `moire_single.c` defines an adapter before
  `single_precision.h` and maps the name to it. Compare the wrapper's frames
  with the unmodified hack's: they were all different here, and identical once
  the adapter was in. A hack with no decimal literals (Moire) must not be in
  `patch_float_literals.py`, which refuses a file without any.

  every 50 ms and holds each picture 5 s; Cynosure waits 500 ms a frame, which
  is upstream's default), so their fps is low whatever the step is. Cynosure's
  `XCreateBitmapFromData`, which the scorer lists as a gap, is inside a
  `DO_STIPPLE` block that is never defined.

  rectangle, an OR/XOR/copy between planes (the GC's `function`, which the shim
  now remembers) and a faster expansion to the window. Upstream's free leaves
  its pixmaps to the X server, and the runner frees only the shim's own, so the
  wrapper frees the planes. The first version ran at 9.6 fps: the plane copy
  and the expansion were 26 and 27 ms, because 64-bit index maths is several
  instructions an operation on a 32-bit core and the expansion branched on
  every pixel. After clipping everything fits an int; a byte table of eight
  pixels written four bytes at a time did the rest (28 ms). The 50 ms delay is
  overridden to 10 ms: 12.6 fps became 16.2.

  squared, and a smaller count makes fewer, larger hexagons over the same area:

  `-DHEXTRAIL_COUNT=<n>`). Rod found 12.7 too slow once the picture filled

  never needs (see `gl.md`) gave 15.3, worst window 10.8. The single-precision

  locals' addresses, which a float rename would write eight bytes (as Moire).

  multiply-add made it slightly negative and the hack's `assert()` aborted

  margins of -600 to -900 left most of a pattern off the screen, one held 1.1

  heap by a model; grid and Kennicott now use minus one edge, and the triangle
  width/2 plus two edges (its incircle is half its circumradius). And it
  scales the 0.0001 animation tick by `CELTIC_STEP_SCALE` (default 4,

  picture's draw calls to 100 / scale. A test bounds a pattern's host bytes
  over 150 starts. Do not shorten `*delay2`: it is a 5 s dwell on the finished
  picture upstream. It looked like a pause on black while the shim's
  `erase_window` cleared first (issue #86); now the first call leaves the
  picture up and the wipe follows the wait. When forcing a graph type in a
  scratch copy to compare, set the margin for that type too, or the triangle
  comes out too small to fill the screen.

  (memcpy, a 2 by 2 blow-up, 32-bit stores). Eruption at half size
  (`eruption_direct.c`, `lowrez_put.h`, `-DERUPTION_SCALE`) spent 26 ms of a
  39 ms step putting its image and 13 ms on the fire. `lowrez_put.h` wants
  ordinary RGB565, so Eruption's palette is swapped at `XAllocColor`.
  Interference changes every pixel each frame; telling it the window is half
  the size changes its look (its wave table is in window pixels), so it stays
  at 10.2 fps.
- Kumppa rotates its picture with `XCopyArea` from the window onto itself.
  The fine checkerboard in its trails is the hack's: copies are checked
  against a read-everything-first reference in every overlap direction.
- Piecewise (`piecewise_direct.c`) is single precision with `single_frand.h`
  (67 to 42 ms) and frees each circle's high fringe, which upstream's free
  forgets (32 blocks a stop; `leaks` named `fringe_add_intersection`).

  16-bit path drops every hit below one 5-bit step, so only green builds up
  and the picture stays dim. Its pixels go straight to the window as it plots
  them, and the frame's `XPutImage` into a pixmap and copy back are skipped:
  the 32-bit image was put a pixel at a time, 130 of a 240 ms step.
  `tools/binaryring_patch.py` makes `frand1`'s exponent literal a float.

  30 fps, so at 10 fps a picture takes about 36 s instead of 12.

  (`tools/etruscanvenus_patch.py`, upstream's 192 by 128) at half resolution;

  try others. Its modes differ: those that fill the screen are fill-bound.
  `curlicue.h` is copied from `vendor/` at build time (`vendor_data.py`).

  `blocktube_patch.py` stay, the wrapper out of the build filter. To bring

  10 ms delay (`"*delay: 10000"` in its registry entry, now gone);

  sets the block's colour, and a block the fog hides is not drawn. There is

  converted from `vendor/` at build time (`gl_textures.py`). It also filters

  frame.

  `failed_ports.txt`). Each Companion Cube face draws a 9,588-vertex disc:

  26,340 vertices (about 630 KB of floats, which would not fit beside the
  current firmware in the 3 MB app partition).

  second batch, then brought back after Rod asked for the shim to be extended.

  depth-1 pixmap it filled with `XFillPolygon`, and the shim drew nothing into

  all but 32 KB of the internal heap while it runs (about 180 of its 400
  bitmaps are under the 4 KB internal limit); a rotation soak that left it for
  DecayScreen read heap and PSRAM back at their idle values. DecayScreen smears

  it stays black. Both were host-only findings from a frame dump: look at later
  frames (3,000) as well as 400 before pinning, and read what the hack draws
  with.
- Penrose (`penrose_short_pause.c`, `tools/penrose_patch.py`) restarts after
  900 frames (about 10 s at 87 fps) instead of 3,141 once the screen is full
  and 31,415 after an error it thinks it can recover from, about six minutes
  at the board's rate with nothing moving. Upstream counts those pauses in
  frames, tuned for a fast X server, so other devices show the same stall.
- Triangle's palette is `make_smooth_colormap`, which the shim now builds the
  way upstream picks it (two to five random colours, any saturation, never
  black): its first version was always a bright rainbow, and every hack that
  asks for a smooth map changed colour with the fix (24 pinned hashes moved,

  in the leak test, but watch it in a rotation soak. Lisa takes 87 ms a step
  as copied (9.6 fps) and 52 ms in single precision (`lisa_single.c`, 14.3

  one pixel wide and there are only a few on a 466 pixel screen: plain, for
  Rod to judge. XRaySwarm's host frames are white bugs and trails; whether
  that is its default look or a colour-table gap in the shim is unchecked.
